problem.title: Every new session starts by searching
problem.body: A new session does not know your layout, so it lists folders, greps and opens files to find its way. Stacklit gives it a map first. In our test the same questions took {grepControl} Grep and Glob calls without the map and {grepArm} with it. The agent can still grep when it needs to.

citation.text: In one study of eight models on SWE-bench Verified, the higher cost runs repeated file views and edits more, and three of the higher cost models repeated around half of their file actions on the same file.
citation.source: Bai et al., How Do AI Agents Spend Your Money? (arXiv 2604.22750)
citation.caveat: This describes the waste in other agents. It is not our result. One preprint, one benchmark.

items.name: Map it
items.text: One command scans the repo with tree-sitter and writes stacklit.json, a dependency diagram and a visual map, then opens the map in your browser.

items.name: Wire it up
items.text: Setup finds the assistants on your machine and writes the config each one reads. It also installs git hooks that rebuild the map after commits, checkouts and merges.

items.name: Ask where
items.text: Your agent asks a plain question and gets a ranked file list that fits a token budget. Slice prints one symbol's source. Impact lists what depends on it.

proof.title: How well does it find the right file?
proof.intro: We asked 47 where-is-it questions over six public repos and checked which file a simple script would open first. No AI model was involved. With one short query, Stacklit put the right file first on 81% of them and in the top five on 96%.
proof.note: Grep with a pattern written by someone who knew the answer did better: 89% first, 100% in the top five. Plain keyword search did worse at the first file, 57%. We tuned Stacklit on these questions, so treat 81% as a best case. On 40 fresh questions from our own repo the right file came first on 28 and in the top five on all 40. No AI model was involved here. The agent results above come from real sessions.
proof.sizes: For scale, the whole map of a repo is {range} tokens. A token is a small chunk of text, about three quarters of a word.

items: Free and MIT. There is no paid tier.
One Go binary that runs on your machine.
No AI model builds the map. The same repo always gives the same map.
One optional command, init --summary, sends module names (never file contents) to a command you choose. It is off by default.
Every number links to its method in the repo, including the ones that make us look worse.

items.q: Will it lower my token bill?
items.a: Not in our test. Across {pairs} pairs of sessions on three repos, the bill stayed about the same. The behaviour changed instead: {grepFewer}% fewer grep and glob searches, a third fewer tool calls, a quarter fewer turns. What a session cost followed the size of the repo. On the largest (about 16,000 files) it fell {levelrailDrop}%. On the smallest (about 400 files) it rose {featuredropRise}%. Questions like "who imports X" cost about {impactRatio} times as much. Dollar figures are Claude Code's own estimates at list prices, for one model and 30 questions we wrote. The full tables are on the agent test page.

No. Answers were slightly less often right with Stacklit: {correctControl}% without it, {correctArm}% with it, on the grader we fixed in advance. After we corrected three grading mistakes of ours it was {auditedControl}% against {auditedArm}%, and that gap could be chance. The losses were mostly on questions that need several files, where the agent stopped after one query. The detail is on the agent test page.

Often grep is enough, and for an exact name it is better: on 'who imports X' questions it was cheaper. Stacklit helps when the question is a plain sentence with no name to grep, and on big repos. In our test agents with the map ran 82% fewer Grep and Glob calls and a third fewer tool calls overall. The map is also one file in git that every assistant reads and a pull request can review.

items.q: Does 82% fewer searches mean 82% less work?
items.a: No. The agent swapped most greps for Stacklit queries. Total tool calls fell by a third and turns by about a quarter. Cost did not change.

items.q: Does it keep the map fresh?
items.a: A git hook rebuilds it after commits, checkouts and merges. In Claude Code an optional hook refreshes it after each edit, and stacklit watch keeps the symbol graph current. Edits made by hand while none of these run wait for the next run. Use stacklit refresh or stacklit generate.

items.q: Does it send my code anywhere?
items.a: No. It runs locally with no account and no telemetry. The one exception is the optional init --summary, which pipes module names and exports, no file contents, to a command you configure. This website makes no third party requests. The generated map pages request small language logos from thesvg.org unless you turn that off with STACKLIT_MAP_ICONS=off.

final.title: Give your agent a map
final.text: One command, free, MIT. Commit the map and every assistant on your team starts from the same page.

meta.title: Stacklit: stop making your AI re-read your codebase
meta.description: Stacklit maps your repo once. In a 450-session test, agents ran 82% fewer grep and glob searches and a third fewer tool calls. Cost unchanged. Free, MIT, one Go binary.
meta.structured: Stacklit is a free, MIT licensed command line tool that writes a small committed map of a codebase for AI coding agents, with token budgeted queries for files, symbols and dependents.
meta.llms: Stacklit writes a small map of your codebase into git so coding agents start from the layout. A 19,500 line Go repo (gin v1.10.0) becomes a 137 token map (tokens are bytes divided by 4). It parses a repository with tree-sitter and writes stacklit.json, a dependency diagram and an interactive HTML map, and sets up 25 assistants including Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. The map is built without an LLM or embeddings. Free, MIT, one Go binary, no account, no telemetry. In our benchmark a 1,000 token query puts the right file first on 81% of questions, and grep with a hand written pattern does better at 89%; it is a benchmark, not an agent study. In a separate test of 450 real Claude Code sessions on three public repos, Stacklit cut tool calls by about a third but did not lower cost overall (cost ratio 1.00, 95% interval 0.93 to 1.07): cheaper on the largest repo, more expensive on the two small ones.

agentTest.title: What happened in real agent sessions
agentTest.intro: We ran Claude Code on three public repos it had not memorised, with and without Stacklit: {sessions} sessions in all, with the plan written down before the first run. Stacklit changed how the agent works. It did not lower the cost.
agentTest.tableCaption: Cost of a session with Stacklit divided by the same session without it, with a 95% interval. Below 1 means cheaper. 50 paired sessions per repo, {pairs} in all. Cost is the CLI's notional list price.
helps: Big repos. On the largest one (about 16,000 files) the bill fell {levelrailDrop}%.
Questions like "where is X?" when you do not know the name.
Questions like "where should a new thing go?"
fails: Small repos. On the two smaller ones the bill stayed the same or went up.
Following a path across several files. Answers were right {traceArm}% of the time with Stacklit, against {traceControl}% without.
Exact names. If you already know the name, plain grep is better. Questions like "who imports X" cost about {impactRatio} times as much with Stacklit.
The strict setup (it blocks the agent from crawling) was worse. It is off by default.
agentTest.limits: Limits: one model (Sonnet), 30 questions we wrote, three repos, one day. Most questions needed only one or two exact greps. Editing tasks, other models and harder reasoning were not tested.
